scope: Wikimedia Commons file-page audit for visually relevant candidate references; no media downloaded locally and no assets approved for use.

candidates.file: 0657 - Museo archeologico di Milano - Calco iscrizione di Pilato da Cesarea, sec. I d.C. - Foto Giovanni Dall'Orto, 12-Mar-2012.jpg
candidates.author: Giovanni Dall'Orto (Commons account G.dallorto)
candidates.license: Attribution-only permission granted by copyright holder; page says any use including commercial/derivative use is allowed if properly attributed. Commons structured data categorizes as attribution-only. Not a named CC version.
candidates.depictedObjectAndDate: 2012 photograph of a cast of the first-century Pilate inscription; file states the original was found at Caesarea and the cast is in Milan's Archaeological Museum.
candidates.recommendedUse: Reference or inset showing a labeled modern cast of the inscription, with an explicit caption that the photograph depicts a cast in Milan, not the archaeological stone at Caesarea.
candidates.anachronismsAndLimits: Do not present as an object currently located at Caesarea or as a photograph of the original. This image is not an ancient image; the cast reproduces a first-century inscription.

candidates.file: Ancient Roman aqueduct in Caesarea Maritima in Israel (1).JPG
candidates.author: Chmee2
candidates.license: Creative Commons Attribution 3.0 Unported (CC BY 3.0); file page also offers GFDL 1.2-or-later option.
candidates.depictedObjectAndDate: Modern photograph dated 8 August 2011 of a Roman-period aqueduct at Caesarea; image geotag 32.512142, 34.896742.
candidates.recommendedUse: Regional landmark / present-day site reference only; not a scene-specific artifact for Pilate's prefecture.
candidates.anachronismsAndLimits: Aqueduct phases are not dated on this file page and the visible structure should not be assumed to have existed in precisely this form in 27–36 CE. Avoid as a close period reconstruction.

candidates.file: The Bath-Gymnasium complex at Sardis, late 2nd - early 3rd century AD, Sardis, Turkey (16480064913).jpg
candidates.author: Carole Raddato (Flickr account Following Hadrian)
candidates.depictedObjectAndDate: Photo dated 2 April 2015. Commons description identifies the structure as the Bath-Gymnasium complex of late second/early third century; image shows the reconstructed Marble Court, reconstructed from fragments in the 1960s–1970s.
candidates.recommendedUse: Possible modern-site reference for the monumental Roman city, provided image label states that the visible Marble Court is a modern archaeological reconstruction.
candidates.anachronismsAndLimits: Not a view of the city in 170–180 CE: the visible court was substantially reassembled in the twentieth century, and the complex is dated slightly later than the Melito episode. Do not imply it is a documented Christian meeting place or synagogue.

candidates.author: Dosseman
candidates.depictedObjectAndDate: Modern photograph dated 13 December 2004; Commons description dates initial synagogue construction to 230–250 CE and renovation to the fourth century.
candidates.recommendedUse: Useful only for later Jewish communal continuity in Sardis, if relevant to a later episode; unsuitable for a 170–180 CE Melito episode without strong date caveat.
candidates.anachronismsAndLimits: Building dates are the Commons description, not a directly inspected excavation report. The page says substantial restoration makes original and restored fabric difficult to distinguish. Later than Melito's proposed lifetime/event.

candidates.author: Zde
candidates.depictedObjectAndDate: Modern photograph dated 28 September 2020; Commons caption identifies Temple E / Temple of Octavia and dates it to the early first century CE.
candidates.recommendedUse: Best of these candidates as a Roman-period city landmark near Paul's conventional Corinthian stay around 50–52 CE, with attribution and an explicit archaeological-site caption.
candidates.anachronismsAndLimits: Dedication to Octavia is not secure; Temple E is a conventional alias and the identification/dedication is debated. It is not evidence of Paul's presence at the temple or of a Christian assembly there.

candidates.author: MM
candidates.license: Public domain, released by the photographer without conditions to the extent permitted by law.
candidates.depictedObjectAndDate: Modern photograph of the Temple of Apollo at Ancient Corinth; photo dated April 2006. The monument is archaic (sixth century BCE), though the Roman city later reused and altered the area.
candidates.recommendedUse: Generic geography/landmark image only, not as a representative Roman-period building for c.50 CE.
candidates.anachronismsAndLimits: The standing archaic columns predate Paul's stay by centuries; Roman-period modifications are not visible enough to treat this as a reconstruction of the first-century urban setting.

methodNotes: Each Commons description page was opened and checked for authorship, stated license and file caption; thumbnail/original URL values were checked against Wikimedia Commons imageinfo API response.
Licensing metadata is transcribed as stated on the file page; verify the live source page again at final use, retain attribution and license links, and indicate modifications.
No image has been selected or downloaded into the workspace; these are research candidates only.
